title: A Rhetoric of Motives — Book-Level Ontology
author: Kenneth Burke

tier_legend.1: Spine / architectonic — the master terms Burke's rhetorical system is built on; foregrounded in Phase 0 briefing as default Tier-1
tier_legend.2: Major structural — significant working concepts given extended analysis; appear in multiple units
tier_legend.3: Supporting / local — concepts whose function is unit-specific or terminological scaffolding

concepts.label: Identification
concepts.gloss: Burke's master term for rhetoric: A is identified with B when their interests are (or are persuaded to be) joined, making them consubstantial while each remains a distinct locus of motives. Replaces 'persuasion' as the governing term because it captures the intermediate rhetorical area between full deliberateness and full unconscious expression. Encompasses property-identification, autonomous-specialty identification, self-address, faction belonging, and ultimate mystical union as species.

concepts.label: Consubstantiality / Consubstantiation
concepts.gloss: The substance-theoretic ground of identification: to identify A with B is to make them 'substantially one' while each remains a distinct locus. Grounded in the claim that 'substance' was originally an act — a way of life is an 'acting-together' in which people share sensations, concepts, images, ideas, and attitudes that make them consubstantial. Extended across units from person/person to person/faction, person/class, actor/universal-developmental-principle, and finally mystical union.

concepts.label: Attitude (Incipient Act) — 6th Dramatistic Term
concepts.gloss: Burke's seeding of a sixth dramatistic term beyond the Grammar's pentad. Rhetorical language is inducement to action 'or to attitude, attitude being an incipient act' (p.42). A leaning or orientation that is not yet overt conduct; more general and foundational as a rhetorical target than action itself. In its mystic culmination (RM-07), all nervous impulses 'attitudinally glow' simultaneously — the pure incipience of ultimate identification.

concepts.label: Mystery
concepts.gloss: The rhetorical condition arising where different kinds of beings communicate across a structural social divide. Requires both strangeness and the possibility of communion; generated by any pronounced social distinction — rank, class, age, race. Not subjective feeling but an objective structural effect of hierarchic difference. Ranges from embarrassment and glamour through military-caste aura to theological opacity. At its limit (RM-07), identification pushed absolutely becomes mystical.

concepts.label: Hierarchy
concepts.gloss: The eulogistic word for bureaucracy and the universal motivational-symbolic principle organizing existence on a scale of higher/lower. Inevitable in systematic thought; reversible at the level of pure principle. Generates courtship, mystery, and mystification as its systematic effects. In RM-05, hierarchy becomes the formal structure of an 'ultimate vocabulary' — the guiding-idea or principle of principles that ranks competing dialectical voices.

concepts.label: Courtship
concepts.gloss: The rhetorical principle operative whenever beings of different social kinds communicate; rhetoric generated wherever hierarchy structures relations. Not primarily sexual but structural — uses mystery's opacity as its suasive resource. Ranges from Castiglione's classical paradigm through Kafka's grotesque caricature to Kierkegaard's perpetual courtship (renunciation and advance fused in one attitude). The abstract paradigm of all persuasion when hierarchy is present.

concepts.label: The Negative
concepts.gloss: Division as the ironic counterpart of identification — 'rhetoric is concerned with the state of Babel after the Fall' (p.23). Identification is affirmed with earnestness precisely because there is division; pure identification would eliminate strife. The negative also structures: the Kill and victimage (hierarchy generates guilt that seeks discharge), mystification (the specific concealed by the generic), and dialectical terms whose meaning shifts by contrast.

concepts.label: Pure Persuasion
concepts.gloss: The limit-concept of rhetoric: the saying of something for a satisfaction intrinsic to the saying, not for extraverbal advantage. Exists nowhere in absolute form but is present as a motivational ingredient in any rhetoric. Its formal hallmark is self-interference or standoffishness: a persisting persuasive act requires its own self-interference, because when the plea is answered persuasion ends. Culminates dialectically in prayer as pure beseeching addressed to the god-term itself.

concepts.label: Terministic Screen
concepts.gloss: Each vocabulary order constitutes a screen directing and deflecting attention: positive screen is physicalist/perceptual; dialectical screen is partisan/polar; ultimate screen ranks motives hierarchically. Switching screens changes what counts as a motive. First operative (unnamed) in RM-00's imaging-of-transformation analysis; named and systematized in RM-03's terministic-reservation and fully theorized in RM-05's three-vocabulary-orders framework.

concepts.label: Ultimate Identification
concepts.gloss: The apex of the identification arc: identification pushed to its dialectical limit becomes mystical union — dissolution of the individual into boundless being, consubstantiality with the universal order. Characterized by William James's composite mystic portrait as the motive heading in 'God as the beloved cynosure and sinecure, the end of all desire' (p.333). Distinguished from Ersatzmystik (substitute mysticisms) that deform the same drive into demonic purpose.

concepts.label: Imaging of Transformation
concepts.gloss: Transformation is the ground-motive; killing/suicide/self-immolation are one family of available images for localizing it. Includes Upward/Downward Way, Exile/Homecoming, seasonal cycles as equally valid alternatives. The specific image chosen is a terministic screen revealing motivational character.

concepts.label: Motivational Recipe
concepts.gloss: The total complex of motivational ingredients in their proportions and contextual qualifications. Cannot be reduced to a single 'gist' without misrepresenting the whole. The qualifying modifiers supplied by dramatic context are themselves constitutive of the motive as a whole.

concepts.label: Dramatic and Philosophic Terms for Essence
concepts.gloss: Narrative/temporal translation of philosophical essence-claims: the end of a story formally declares essence. Opposed to but formally homologous with philosophic terms (entelechy, abstract finishedness); mutually convertible by heuristic reversal. Includes temporizing of essence (ancestral or culminative pole).

concepts.label: Rhetoric as Addressed (incl. Self-Address)
concepts.gloss: Persuasion implies an audience; a man can be his own audience ('an I addressing its me,' Mead). The psyche is a parliament; socialization presses from without while the individual completes it from within. 'Only those voices from without are effective which can speak in the language of a voice within' (p.39). Rhetoric's realistic function — inducing cooperation in symbol-responsive beings — is grounded here.

concepts.label: Formal Appeal
concepts.gloss: The persuasive power of rhetorical form as such, independent of propositional content. Purely formal structures arouse collaborative expectancy in audiences, priming assent to whatever content occupies the formal slots. Form is itself a rhetorical motive, not mere embellishment.

concepts.label: Image as Identification-Node
concepts.gloss: The image is 'built of identifications' (p.85): it condenses multiple organizing principles simultaneously, so translating an ideological argument into an image yields an 'unearned increment' of associated meaning — consubstantiality not explicitly contracted in the argument. Image and idea are continuous, both serving identification.

concepts.label: Imagination (Rhetorical Function)
concepts.gloss: Genealogical treatment from Aristotle through Bacon to Hazlitt. Imagination as the immediate spring of action and ground of identification through anticipatory proximity: we identify more readily with what we can imaginatively inhabit. Rhetoric applies reason to imagination to move will (Bacon).

concepts.label: Triplicate Vocabulary (Bentham)
concepts.gloss: Every domain of motive yields a neutral term flanked by eulogistic and dyslogistic counterparts. The neutral ideal is never a rhetorical reality; uninflected vocabulary cannot induce action. The eulogistic/dyslogistic poles are the normal condition of motivated discourse. Includes the censorial appellative — a word carrying evaluative weight as though descriptive.

concepts.label: Covering Motive (tegumen / res tegenda)
concepts.gloss: When the actual motive behind an act cannot be presented eulogistically, a speaker selects the most favorable co-operative motive and presents it as the whole or essence. The linguistic veil (tegumen) over the interest concealed (res tegenda). Links Bentham's vocabulary analysis to Burke's theory of identification.

concepts.label: Mystification
concepts.gloss: The rhetorical operation (Marx's dyslogistic term) by which specific class interests are concealed beneath apparently universal or spiritual motive-terms. The ideological substitution of generic for specific. Paired against Carlyle's eulogistic 'mystery': both address the same social phenomenon (hierarchy generating rhetorical difference) from opposite evaluative stances.

concepts.label: God-Term
concepts.gloss: A high-abstraction summarizing word — 'honor,' 'liberty,' 'Providence,' 'Absolute Idea' — gathering a complex of material conditions under a single spiritualized label. In RM-05, the apex term that ranks all other motives in an ultimate vocabulary. In RM-07, the terminus of dialectical ascent: from positive words, through titles, to title-of-titles. Burke's inventory lists substance, nature, history, society, logos, hierarchy, authority, consubstantiality, nation, freedom, pure persuasion as surrogate god-terms.

concepts.label: Imitation
concepts.gloss: The master dramatistic concept subsuming competition, emulation, and the invidious; makes for consubstantiality by community of ways. Competition = out-imitation. The symbolic motive is more general than the pecuniary; laws of symbols are prior to any particular property structure. Veblen's 'invidious' is a partisan special case.

concepts.label: Administrative Rhetoric
concepts.gloss: Rhetoric that includes nonverbal, material operations — spectacles, military force, institutional apparatus — as well as verbal address. Nonverbal conditions persuade by their symbolic meaning, not merely material effect. Burke's reading of Machiavelli's Prince as a manual of administrative rhetoric is the worked example.

concepts.label: Socioanagogic Method
concepts.gloss: Secular adaptation of the medieval anagogical sense: reading social hierarchy where divine or erotic imagery appears on the surface. Positioned midway between Marx's rage at mystification and Carlyle's adulation of mystery. Treats a text's known moral/social judgments as transparent to disclose the hierarchic content of its imagery.

concepts.label: Three Vocabulary Orders (Positive / Dialectical / Ultimate)
concepts.gloss: Positive terms: names grounded in perception, locatable hic et nunc (Bentham's real entities). Dialectical terms: polar vocabulary whose meaning shifts by contrast (Bentham's fictitious entities). Ultimate terms: a guiding-idea or principle of principles that places competing dialectical voices in a developmental hierarchy. Conflating the orders produces terministic impropriety; rhetoric operates primarily at the dialectical and ultimate levels.

concepts.label: Marxist Persuasion (as Ultimate Vocabulary Case Study)
concepts.gloss: Burke's primary case study in ultimate vocabulary. Rhetorical power derives from arranging classes in a developmental hierarchy grounded in the universe itself, enabling any local participation to be simultaneously particular and universal (Hegelian concrete universal). The worker identified with 'the Proletarian' participates in the total dialectic of historical development.

concepts.label: Mythic Ground
concepts.gloss: Motivational level transcending discursive reason, figured in image rather than idea. In Platonic dialogue, the culminating mythic image figures a motive the dialectical ascent has prepared one to receive. Mannheim's error is treating mythic ground as equivalent to ideological bias; doing so eliminates the primary motive power along with the biases.

concepts.label: Sociology of Knowledge (Mannheim)
concepts.gloss: Mannheim's 'relationist' project: systematic discounting of ideological bias by studying connections between ideologies and their nonverbal conditions. Burke classifies it as 'pro-ultimate' — more precise than relativism but unable to reach genuine ultimate order because it lacks a governing principle of principles.

concepts.label: Embarrassment and Glamour
concepts.gloss: Involuntary self-constraint triggered by hierarchic difference (embarrassment) and the quasi-magical perceptual magnification produced by hierarchic radiance (glamour — from 'gramarye,' necromancy). Both are evidence of mystery in social intercourse: the sign of different social kinds in contact.

concepts.label: The Kill / Victimage
concepts.gloss: The mechanism by which hierarchy discharges the guilt it generates: invidious distinction produces accumulated moral pressure, discharged through scapegoating a sacrificial victim. The Kill is not the essence; common participation in a solemn experience is. The Rattlesnake Club anecdote is the paradigm: boys bonded by a shared notable experience, quickly fracturing into hierarchic cliques.

concepts.label: Range of Mountings
concepts.gloss: Ideal paradigm for the symbol of ascending: kinesthetic, erotic, maternal, social-careerism, ethical, fecal-scatological, anagogic, and mystical-absolute strands. Maximum symbolic vibrancy obtains when all strands are simultaneously operative in a single symbol. Burke applies this to Hopkins, Yeats, Eliot, and Dante's Purgatorio.

concepts.label: Principle of the Oxymoron
concepts.gloss: The mystic communicates in the oxymoron because mystic experience is the simultaneous glow of contradictory impulses — a condition of radical passivity in which all nervous impulses 'attitudinally glow' at once without the repression required for ordinary purposive action. The oxymoron is the literary analogue of this non-repressive condition.

concepts.label: Homo Dialecticus
concepts.gloss: Man as the 'classifying animal' whose formal aptitude for classification is prior to social classification; social hierarchy is a special case of this general formal ground. Contrasted with homo faber (tool-using). Grounds Burke's argument that psychoanalytic and institutional explanations conceal the formal/dialectical priority.

concepts.label: Grammar–Rhetoric–Symbolic Triad
concepts.gloss: Burke's three-volume architecture: Grammar built on 'substance' (universal paradoxes/placement); Rhetoric on identification ('substance' applied to persuasion/dissuasion); Symbolic to be built on 'identity' (unique individuals at peace). Consubstantiality bridges Grammar to Rhetoric; identification bridges Rhetoric to Symbolic.

concepts.label: Magic as Primitive Rhetoric / Faulty Derivation
concepts.gloss: Word-magic reverses the true order: the realistic use of addressed language to induce action in people was mistakenly transferred to induce motion in things; magic is a faulty derivation from rhetoric, not its ancestor. Magic's socializing aspect is better read as 'primitive rhetoric' promoting social cohesion (Malinowski, Kluckhohn).

concepts.label: Advantage / Agonistic Rhetoric
concepts.gloss: Burke's proposed master-term for subsuming all classical variants of rhetorical purpose and scientific psychological terminologies of drives. Rhetoric shaped by a strongly competitive purpose: proving opposites, countering jest with earnest. Related to Aristotle's view of rhetoric as 'the faculty of discovering persuasive means in a given case.'

concepts.label: Literature for Use
concepts.gloss: Literary works performing rhetorical-political work: overtly (Areopagitica) or at one remove (Samson — ritual and magic order). Demonstrates that the range of rhetoric extends from bluntest propaganda through courtship, etiquette, education, sermon to 'pure persuasion' — appeal enjoyed for its own sake.

concepts.label: Rhetorica Utens / Rhetorica Docens
concepts.gloss: Standard scholastic distinction: rhetoric comprises both the USE of persuasive resources (rhetorica utens, Demosthenes) and the STUDY of them (rhetorica docens, Aristotle's Art of Rhetoric). Burke uses this pair to define rhetoric's scope before expanding it through identification.

concepts.label: Context of Situation (Malinowski)
concepts.gloss: Nonverbal situational factors that participate in a rhetorical act's effectiveness. Generalizes the requirement that meaning cannot be separated from nonverbal scene. Applied in RM-03 to qualify the Marxist diagnostic (terministic reservation) and in RM-05 to demonstrate that even positivistic reduction contains a minimal mythic element.

Grammar_of_Motives.notes: Rhetoric extends and operationalizes the Grammar's 'substance' into identification; attitude-incipient-act seeds the 6th dramatistic term. Scene-act, agent-act ratios cross-referenced throughout.

Calleja_In_Game.primary_bridge: consubstantiality <-> incorporation (IG-10): both name the dynamic of a being made substantially one with something other than itself while remaining a distinct locus. Functional homology, not lexical.
